paras: The expulsion of Black pipe line workers from Sour Lake took place in early February 1903, when white men at the Texas oil field ordered the Black employees of a pipe line contractor to leave under threat of being driven away or killed. All twenty-five Black workers left, most of them for Beaumont, and the one who spoke to a reporter said he saw no motive, since the Black men were paid more than the whites.

Contractor John Kinsley was building a pipe line from the Sour Lake field toward the railway, employing both white and Black laborers. A Beaumont correspondent described what followed as "a serious development of labor troubles" between the two groups.

About February 3, one of "a number of white men" at Sour Lake sent a note that was handed to Will Kinsley, the contractor's son. Signed only "WE," it stated that the Black workers must leave by noon the next day or "trouble could be expected," and it intimated that they would be driven away or "killed outright." The twenty-five Black employees, all those affected by the notice, left on February 4, and most went to Beaumont.

On February 5 John Kinsley was in Beaumont trying to persuade the men to return. The worker interviewed refused, saying "his hide was a little too thin to withstand harsh treatment" and that the others felt the same, and he withheld his name for fear "it might go hard with him." Kinsley had not said what he would do, and the coverage shows no arrests, no official inquiry and no identification of the note's authors.

The only report found is a Beaumont dispatch in the Houston Daily Post of February 6, carried in its "Budget from Beaumont" column under the headline "Negro Workman Driven Away from the Sour Lake Pipe Line." The dispatch rested on the account of one departed worker and reported his point that Black men earned $15 a week against $2 a day for whites without adding comment of its own. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black pipe line workers from Sour Lake, Texas (February 1903)
bases: A written note from white men ordered the Black workers on the pipe line to leave by a deadline under threat of being driven away or killed, and all twenty-five left (A1).
Only the Houston Daily Post's Beaumont dispatch reports the episode, and its account comes from one of the departed workers (A1).

accounts.label: Departed Black worker, via Beaumont correspondent
accounts.gist: A note signed "WE" ordered the Black workers out by noon or face being driven away or killed; all twenty-five left. He saw no motive, since Black workers got $15 a week and whites $2 a day.

framing.detail: The Houston Daily Post ran it in a "Budget from Beaumont" column under "Negro Workman Driven Away from the Sour Lake Pipe Line," calling it "labor troubles" and giving the worker's account without comment.

record_check.dossier: Twenty-five unnamed Black employees of contractor John Kinsley
Unnamed white men at Sour Lake ("a number of white men"); one sent the note signed "WE"
No mob gathered; a group of white men, apparently fellow workers on the pipe line, acted by written note
The note was signed "WE" (not unsigned); delivered about Feb. 3 with a noon Feb. 4 deadline; workers left Feb. 4
No county is named in the coverage

info: Note delivered about Feb. 3, 1903 ("day before yesterday" in a Feb. 5 dispatch); deadline noon Feb. 4; workers left Feb. 4

Twenty-five Black ("colored") employees of contractor John Kinsley, unnamed
"A number of white men there"; one of them sent the note, signed "WE"; none named

set_aside: AP, Sour Lake, July 9: notices posted warning all Black residents to leave after a brakeman was shot at Rome Junction; separate episode.
New Orleans, Sept. 17: notices at Sour Lake ordering Black residents out, said to be a practical joker's; separate episode.
